description: Linux Security Summit North America talks from Linux Security Summit North America 2024.

talks.title: Protecting the Linux Kernel from Confidential Computing Threats...
talks.teaser: Carlos Bilbao examines Protecting the Linux Kernel from Confidential Computing Threats....
talks.summary:
Overview: Elena and Carlos present at Linux Security Summit North America on protecting the Linux kernel in confidential computing environments, sharing their experience submitting backports.

Key Topics: Confidential computing threat models for cloud workloads; protection in transit and at rest versus gaps during processing; kernel community pushback on confidential computing patches; and aligning security fixes with upstream philosophy.

Technical Details: Presenters describe submitting PCI subsystem buffer overflow fixes for confidential computing threat models, receiving pushback that Linux wasn't designed for these threat models. They discuss navigating kernel community expectations while addressing TEE-specific vulnerabilities.

Takeaways: Confidential computing introduces threat models the Linux kernel wasn't originally designed for. Security researchers must engage constructively with kernel maintainers to build appropriate protections.

talks.title: Securing Confidential VMs with COCONUT-SVSM
talks.teaser: Jörg Rödel explores Securing Confidential VMs with COCONUT-SVSM.
talks.summary:
COCONUT-SVSM Overview

SUSE maintainer Joerg Roedel introduces the open-source COCONUT Secure VM Service Module, a platform for secure hypervisor services in confidential VMs. Started as a 2022 prototype, it booted Linux guests in CVMs by early 2023, gained filesystem support, multitasking, TPM emulation, CI testing, 23 contributors, and Confidential Computing Consortium onboarding.

Confidential VM Threat Model

Untrusted hypervisors normally manage guest memory, intercepts, interrupts, and device emulation— exposing data and register-state attacks. Hardware extensions (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX, Arm CCA, RISC-V CVME) encrypt memory and detect remap/replay tampering; some intercepts trap into guest kernels instead of the host.

SVSM’s Role

Where hardware cannot fully mitigate hypervisor functionality, guest-side code can absorb tasks. COCONUT-SVSM implements services that complement hardware protections on x86 and analogous architectures, extending confidential computing beyond raw memory encryption toward practical guest-controlled security modules.

talks.title: Mitigating Integer Overflow in C
talks.teaser: Kees Cook investigates Mitigating Integer Overflow in C.
talks.summary:
Why Integer Overflows Persist

Kees Cook of the Linux kernel self-protection project argues integer overflows remain a root cause of vulnerabilities despite mitigations like control-flow integrity that only catch downstream effects. CVE analysis shows hundreds of medium-and-higher kernel overflow issues over the past decade with little meaningful reduction.

C Semantics and Compiler Traps

Unsigned overflow must wrap per the C standard, while signed overflow is undefined behavior that modern optimizers exploit, eliminating checks like "if (value + offset < value)". The kernel adopted -fno-strict-overflow to force predictable wraparound, but that disables signed-integer-overflow sanitizers that only fire on undefined cases.

Sanitizer Paradox

Clang and GCC offer signed and unsigned overflow sanitizers with warn or trap modes. Cook highlights the absurdity: -fno-strict-overflow makes signed overflow defined, silencing UBSan, while the unsigned sanitizer reports wraps that are legal behavior. Kernel developers need instrumentation regardless of standard semantics.

Path Forward

The talk surveys saturation strategies such as refcount_t, trapping on unexpected overflow, and ongoing efforts to make overflow detection workable alongside kernel build flags. Cook calls for treating arithmetic bounds as a first-class hardening problem rather than relying solely on memory-safe languages elsewhere.

talks.title: Control Flow Integrity on RISC-V Linux
talks.teaser: Deepak Gupta explores Control Flow Integrity on RISC-V Linux.
talks.summary:
CFI motivation on RISC-V

Security engineer "debug" from Revos describes bringing control-flow integrity to RISC-V Linux for data-center workloads. Drawing on prior work at AWS, Intel (including CET-related ISA work), and McAfee, he explains how memory corruption enables attackers to hijack indirect control-flow transfers.

Software and hardware precedents

Existing mitigations include LLVM CFI, SafeStack, Microsoft Control Flow Guard, and x86 CET shadow stacks that validate return addresses. RISC-V lacks identical hardware features, so the Linux community must adapt CFI concepts to RISC-V instruction formats and calling conventions.

RISC-V-specific challenges

RISC-V's variable-length encodings and 20-bit immediate limits in J-type branches constrain how jump targets are encoded. Features like AUIPC enable PC-relative addressing across roughly ±2 GB, affecting how forward-edge and backward-edge protections can be implemented in kernel and userspace code.

talks.title: The Digest_cache LSM
talks.teaser: Shows a kernel LSM that lets integrity checks use package digests, cutting TPM measurement cost and keeping PCR values stable.
talks.summary:
The talk covers the Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) in the Linux kernel, which records file measurements in a TPM-protected list and appraises files by checking their signatures. Two problems are described: measuring with a physical TPM is slow (about 640 microseconds per measurement without a TPM, about 7,000 with a physical TPM and about 1,900 with an emulated one), and PCR values change with the order in which services start, so TPM keys sealed to them stop working after a reboot.

The proposed answer is the Digest Cache LSM, which reads file digests from distribution package metadata, such as RPM headers already signed with PGP, and exposes them to IMA or a BPF LSM. If a file's digest is found in a verified package, IMA skips the measurement and the appraisal succeeds; a file with no matching digest causes attestation to fail. Digest lists are loaded on demand and attached to security blobs, and a deterministic directory scan with sequence-number prefixes keeps the measurement order stable. In benchmarks on Fedora 38, the approach sharply reduced the number of TPM measurements and made appraisal much faster than standard IMA, at the cost of some extra memory.

The speaker acknowledged the trade-off: a remote verifier learns which packages were touched but not which files or in what order. Questions compared the design with measured boot manifests and asked about signed bills of material for allowed package sets, and the speaker noted that other package formats need their own parsers. The practical takeaway is that integrity checks can reuse vendor-signed package data without changing distribution tooling, and that a patch set and a user-space tool are available.

talks.title: Unprivileged Access Control in AppArmor
talks.teaser: Explains how applications can build their own AppArmor policy and map OpenBSD pledge and unveil onto it.
talks.summary:
The talk covers application-directed unprivileged access control in AppArmor, where a program defines its own confinement rather than relying only on a system administrator. The speakers describe a small API that lets an application start from a base profile, confine itself, and later add rules. Policy is compiled into a bounded state machine before loading into the kernel, which makes it verifiable enough for unprivileged users to load. Once loaded, a profile can be locked so it can no longer be replaced.

A major theme is the difficulty of confining multithreaded programs, since each kernel task holds its own credential and profile updates reach sibling threads asynchronously. The speakers then map OpenBSD's pledge and unveil onto AppArmor. Pledge promises can only shrink, so early designs stacked a new profile for each reduction; the team is moving toward locked profiles with runtime Boolean conditionals. Differences in error behaviour, such as killing a process versus returning EACCES or ENOSYS, are handled with per-rule flags. Unveil's directory-tree semantics and directories added after an unveil remain hard cases.

In the questions, the speakers explain that stacked profiles are ordered by policy namespace hierarchy, and that this is a different design from Landlock rather than a rival. They note that BSD forks let semantics drift, which makes cherry-picking patches difficult. The takeaway is that the pledge and unveil mapping is still a work in progress, and a dedicated system call for loading policy is expected later, while a prctl-based interface serves for now.

talks.title: Stacked LSMs and User Space - Casey Schaufler, The Smack Project
talks.teaser: Explains a proposed library that lets applications read and set Linux security module attributes through new system calls.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical gap. Linux security modules attach labels and other attributes to processes, files and other objects, and applications need to read and change them. Until recently the only route was special filesystem entries and /proc/self/attr, which suit shell scripts but are awkward for programs. Newer kernels add LSM system calls that list the active modules and get or set attributes using numeric module IDs instead of name and value string pairs.

The speaker presents a proposed user space library, libLSM, built around those calls. It would include helpers for the LSM context buffer, such as a function to step to the next entry and a function that fills the buffer and handles alignment, along with mappings between module names and IDs and between attribute names and IDs. For older kernels it would emulate the system calls by reading /proc/self/attr, though results cannot match exactly because policies differ. Smack and AppArmor use per-module subdirectories there, while the SELinux maintainers declined one, which complicates emulation. The survey of packages showed 93 Fedora 39 packages with SELinux in the name and 157 depending on libselinux, against 16 and 38 for AppArmor on Ubuntu, with little overlap. Systemd contains an assertion that blocks SELinux and Smack running together, which caused trouble during module stacking tests.

The remaining work includes a new audit record type so that attributes from every stacked module are logged, not just one, and a way to return peer context over network sockets as an LSM context. The main takeaway is to write applications against the system calls instead of module-specific interfaces, so they stay module-agnostic. The library will first be released in a simple form to collect feedback from users.

talks.title: Snapshotting IMA Log
talks.teaser: Explains snapshotting the kernel's IMA measurement log to ease memory pressure while keeping remote attestation verifiable.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at snapshotting the Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) log in Linux. That log lives in kernel memory and keeps growing, because flushing it would break replay against the TPM PCR values used for remote attestation. On long-running servers, such as those in gaming, e-commerce or finance, reboots to free memory are unacceptable, and cloud verifiers need to process large logs quickly.

The proposed design has the kernel emit a snapshot aggregate marker, copy existing entries to a persistent location set by policy, and then truncate the in-memory log while keeping the marker. Snapshots could be triggered by a user-space agent, a kexec boot, or event-count and memory thresholds. A verifier that has already attested earlier snapshots only needs the newer in-memory portion plus later snapshot files. In a live demo, a file open triggered a snapshot, the entries were copied out, and the log was truncated.

The speaker stressed that this change is disruptive: truncating the log before clients and servers support it would cause attestation failures, so the work was first aimed at getting community agreement. Kernel-side truncation was not yet upstream, and the demo used a prototype. The Q&A covered locking, whether user space should handle copying, and a possible handler model, with the maintainers favouring a simple kernel truncate.

talks.title: A Hybrid Alias Analysis Framework and Its Application to Protecting the Linux Kernel
talks.teaser: Presents a pointer analysis that blends data-flow and type-based methods to find which kernel globals can be made read-only.
talks.summary:
Linux kernel exploits often corrupt global variables such as modprobe_path. A hardening mechanism called read-only after init can lock such globals once boot finishes, but it is rarely used. Deciding whether a global is ever written after initialization means knowing every pointer that might reach it, and the rules produced by earlier alias analyses were either unsound or too imprecise for the kernel. Developers had manually tagged only about 500 globals in six years.

The proposed framework is a hybrid alias analysis. It starts with data-flow tracing and, at chosen points, jumps to type-based shortcuts, with the choice of shortcuts adjustable per query and per variable. Type casts are matched at the level of individual objects instead of merging whole types, and pointer arithmetic is normalized to byte offsets, so container_of is handled without a special model. The analysis is built on SVF, answers queries as graph reachability problems, and runs on demand. On kernel 5.4 with the default configuration, it analyzed all roughly 12,000 global variables within a one-hour budget, where a data-flow analysis finished about 3,000. About 5,000 variables were identified as candidates for read-only after init. The speaker reported around 23 false negatives, caused by inline assembly and pointer-to-integer casts. The derived rules also flagged illegal pointers in the recent public exploits that targeted globals.

The main takeaway is that the framework is sound by design except for the undefined-behavior cases noted above. Its output is best used as a list for developers to review, not applied automatically, because marking a variable that is still written as read-only crashes the kernel. The same pointer information could also support other access-control rules and general program analysis tasks.

talks.title: Enhancing Systemd Security Using TPM 2.0
talks.teaser: Explains how systemd's TPM 2.0 session handling let bus attackers capture disk encryption keys, and how the fixes close that gap.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how systemd unlocks LUKS-encrypted disks with a key sealed in a TPM 2.0, and how traffic between the host and the TPM can expose that key. Encrypted TPM sessions are the standard mitigation, but systemd's first session support created a key pair inside the TPM without verifying the public key it received. An attacker on the bus could substitute their own key, decrypt the session and read the disk key while the host never noticed.

The release that followed added a bind key that used the PIN as a shared secret, but recorded traffic could then be attacked offline, which is weak for short PINs. Later fixes strengthened the PIN with a PBKDF2-style derivation using HMAC-SHA256 and a salt stored in the LUKS metadata. The final fix, in version 254, records the TPM object's name at enrollment, similar to trusting an SSH host fingerprint, so sessions are protected even without a PIN. The work also replaced per-operation primary key creation with the storage root key, which avoids requiring the owner password.

The main lesson is to verify any key used to start a TPM session, and to use the feature API or the enhanced system API with proper object names. Remaining work includes sealing over an encrypted session and PCR policies, though the speaker warned that unmeasured components such as systemd itself could be swapped to capture PINs. Users on older versions should upgrade to 254 or later.
